title: Code fence lines are fully hidden in .qmd buffers unless a .md file was opened first
description:
In a `.qmd` buffer, the opening and closing lines of a fenced code block (```` ```python ```` / ```` ``` ````) are completely hidden unless the cursor is on them. If I first open any `.md` file in the same session and then open the `.qmd`, the fence lines are shown normally (screenshots below).

**Findings**

- The hiding seems to come from nvim-treesitter's markdown `highlights.scm`, which sets `conceal` and `conceal_lines` on `fenced_code_block_delimiter` and the `info_string` language.
- With `set conceallevel=0` the fences reappear, so it's treesitter conceal, not syntax conceal (`syntax` is empty, `synconcealed()` returns `0`).
- The query file used is the same in both states.
- Manually loading render-markdown.nvim in the broken state (`:Lazy load render-markdown.nvim`) changes nothing, and its `file_types` doesn't include `quarto`. So opening a markdown file triggers something else that affects `.qmd` buffers.

**Workaround**

Creating a scratch buffer with `filetype=markdown` once, on the first `quarto` FileType event, fixes it:

```lua
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", {
  -- When opening a quarto file with quarto-nvim, first trigger a load with render-markdown to ensure its proper initialization.
  -- This works around an issue where loading a quarto file before markdown results in concealed code block fences.
  pattern = "quarto",
  once = true,
  callback = function()
    local scratch = vim.api.nvim_create_buf(false, true)
    vim.bo[scratch].filetype = "markdown"
    vim.schedule(function()
      vim.api.nvim_buf_delete(scratch, { force = true })
    end)
  end,
})
```

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Start Neovim and open a `.qmd` file containing a Python code block.
2. Move the cursor off the fence lines: they disappear.
3. Open any `.md` file, then delete the `.qmd` buffer and reopen it: the fences are visible.

**Environment**

- Neovim: 0.12.4
- OS: macOS
- Distribution: LazyVim
- quarto-nvim / nvim-treesitter / render-markdown.nvim: v2.1.0 / e289100 / 245956d
- Config: `ft = "quarto", opts = { codeRunner = { enabled = true, default_method = "molten", }, }`

title: [Feature Request] Use w/o `lspconfig`
description:
I'm putting together a config that uses the [native neovim LSP configuration](https://neovim.io/doc/user/lsp.html), _without_ `lspconfig` (or `mason`). Since my life is primarily a stack of Quarto documents at this point, being able to use the handy functionality provided by `quarto-nvim` is close to my heart.

Unfortunately, as far as I know, it is impossible to use `quarto-nvim` without `lspconfig`, since one of the very first things `quarto-nvim` does is `local util = require 'lspconfig.util'`. As far as I can tell, the _only_ reason this is done is to access the root directory: `local root_dir = util.root_pattern '_quarto.yml'(buffer_path)`.

I was hoping you might **consider removing the hard-dependency** on `lspconfig`, by allowing the project root to be found by some other means (ex. a "you're on your own" config option where I provide my own `root_dir` finding logic).

Thank you for your time, and for `quarto-nvim`!
-Sof

# What's Wrong with `lspconfig`?
Well, nothing. It's great! I refer to it frequently when configuring `nvim`. It is, however, opinionated. And its opinions differ from mine 😛 .

`nvim`'s LSP system is itself not so opinionated (the slogan of `nvim`, perhaps). Perhaps not quite opinionated enough. As of recently, however, it seems that `nvim` can increasingly do more and more of the "really important" parts of `lspconfig`'s job, like finding root folders based on markers and/or a custom function. It also seems that there's far less plumbing in today's nightly `nvim`. So I ask, why should I bring in in a massive plugin like `lspconfig`, which itself has a lot of nuanced functionality, for something `nvim` actually already does sufficiently?

My point is not so much to convince anybody, or claim "`lspconfig` is bad now". My point is there are valid reasons why it may **not always desirable** to use `lspconfig`, and that the flexibility of catering to this may be worth the effort!

## But Isn't Non-`lspconfig` LSP Pretty Low Level?
Not really - though resources can be sparse, since `lspconfig` style configs dominates search engine results.

Suppose one wants `ruff` integration. Just `uv tool install ruff`, then create this auto-discovered file:
```lua
-- ~/.config/nvim/lsp/ruff.lua
return {
	cmd = { 'ruff', 'server' },
	filetypes = { 'python' },
	root_markers = { "pyproject.toml" },
}
```

Then, one just needs an `LspAttach` autocmd:
```lua
-- ~/.config/nvim/init.lua (or somewhere that makes you happy)
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('LspAttach', {
	callback = function(args)
            -- Retreive LSP Client & Buffer
            local lsp_client = vim.lsp.get_client_by_id(args.data.client_id)
            local buf = args.buf

            -- Implement LSP-Backed Commands/Keymaps/etc. .
            if lsp_client:supports_method(...) then
                ...
            end
        end
})
```

The [official LSP docs](https://neovim.io/doc/user/lsp.html#lsp-api) helps fill in the blanks, including examples of how to wire up `textDocument/formatting`.

## But Doesn't `otter.nvim` require `lspconfig` Too?
Officially, sure. As it turns out, when `write_to_disk = true`, the `require('lspconfig')` doesn't seem to be called. Apart from that, an autocmd on `FileType` that calls `require('otter').activate()` seems to transitively jiggle `LspAttach` just fine.

Here's my (seemingly) working `lazy.nvim` config:
```lua
return {
	'jmbuhr/otter.nvim',
	commit = "0e42fa795c35c7190935e3beda3791189c41bb72",
	lazy = true,

	init = function()
		vim.treesitter.language.register("markdown", { "quarto", "rmd" })

		vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('FileType', {
			pattern = { 'quarto' },
			callback = function(ev)
				require('otter').activate()
			end
		})
	end,

	opts = {
		buffers = {
			set_filetype = true,
			write_to_disk = true,
		},
	},
}

```

title: Possible fix for LSP Error : Too Many Blank Lines.
description:
**The Problem** : To my current understanding, quarto allows for integrating code into .qmd files by creating invisible buffers for each code chunk, where everything outside the chunk in replaced with blank lines. This causes the LSP linters (tested in python) to show a warning for leaving too many blank lines in the code. 

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/74ae7a98-2096-47cb-b3a2-a87ebffe2bac)

**The suggested fix**: Instead of using blank lines, use empty comments for that language so that all previous lines still exist and the line numbers are preserved, but ignored by the LSP. Thus this will keep the linters functionality to stay inside code chunks only.

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8829a24d-8c0e-4dc3-8fc8-30b1969354a9)
As you can see, commented lines do not trigger the linter.

**Possible Benefits**: Instead of creating multiple invisible buffers, the file can simply be structured so that all other content is ignored with use of comments. This will possibly help ai based completion to be more reliable by using commented lines as valuable context (which in most cases will be explaining the code), and also allows for plugins to generate markdown right into the file(maybe?) using comments like documentation generation.

title: treesitter-text-objects queries overwritten for python, r, bash, markdown
description:
Hi @jmbuhr,

it seems that with some recent updates to treesitter or treesitter-text-objects, the `queries/` folder in `quarto-nvim` plugin seems to be overwriting the `treesitter-text-objects`. I have found [this issue](https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter-textobjects/issues/370) directly pointing to the definitions in the `queries` folder as a culprit of text objects not working. One of the `text-objects` maintainers says that:

> In the quarto-nvim plugin, there's queries/python/textobjects.scm which completely overwrites the nvim-treesitter-textobjects's queries. If you want to extend the queries, you need to have it on after/queries/python/textobjects.scm. For some reason, the plugin just uses both files, and maybe the previous version of this plugin ignored this issue.

I'm not sure if such behavior of treesitter is not a regression, though. According to the official treesitter [docs](https://github.com/nvim-treesitter/nvim-treesitter#adding-queries):

>All queries found in the runtime directories will be combined. By convention, if you want to write a query, use the queries/ directory, but if you want to extend a query use the after/queries/ directory.

My reading of this is that the queries/ directories of all plugins should be somehow combined, but not overwriting each other.

Still, I can confirm that deleting the queries/ folder in quarto-nvim fixes the issue. Maybe these queries can be moved to after/queries folder?

I'm running nvim 0.9.0 and the freshest version of the mentioned packages. I'm running my own custom config (I'm not using the kickstarter-quarto-nvim plugin)

title: [BUG] `QuartoPreview`/`QuartoRender` fail to run unless `$PATH` is updated
description:
Hi! I don't really know which direction will quarto development take, but as of now `quarto` on macOS is installed under 
`/Applications/quarto/bin/quarto`. This means that, unless the user sets `export PATH="/Applications:$PATH`, the `QuartoPreview`/`QuartoRender` commands will fail.

If this behaviour is okay, I could write a PR to make this clearer in the docs. Otherwise, I believe this is the line/location where the magic happens:

https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-nvim/blob/7736a621a1c135a781fd3bb563c341b5f5f145c7/lua/quarto/init.lua#L38

I don't really know where quarto is installed on Windows, but I guess it would be easy to add a conditional ( e.g., if os is macOS, `local quarto_path = '/Applications/quarto/bin'`, else...) and make `local cmd = quarto_path .. '/quarto preview'`. I'd be glade to write this PR as well.
